strong.text: You held the primary survey together: the order, the chest look-alikes, the shock signs and the exam-key conflicts. Your first answers show you ranking by speed of death and checking the qualifier before the habit. Keep the review cards on a spaced schedule so the old-key answers (2 L, 2nd space) do not creep back under exam pressure.

mixed.text: Parts of the primary survey are solid and parts are not yet. The pattern in the sections below shows where you reached for a familiar rule (loudest problem first, usual test first, old key) instead of asking what kills fastest or which qualifier applies. Start with the objectives marked gap or shaky, then the review cards.

weak.text: Several core areas of the primary survey are still open, and that is useful information, not a verdict. The common thread is usually one habit: ranking by what is visible, familiar or printed in older books. Work the review cards in the order listed, and for each card say aloud what kills in minutes before you choose.

secure.text: You ranked the steps by speed of killing: airway, then breathing, then circulation, even with bleeding in view.

shaky.text: Your order was mostly right but not steady. Hold the rule: loss of airway kills faster than loss of breathing, which kills faster than loss of blood volume, so ABCDE follows time to death. Redo the order card once.

gap.text: The first step and the ABCDE order are not yet reliable. Rebuild from one rule: treat the greatest threat to life first, and airway kills fastest. Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable death, but that is frequency, not speed. Start with the O1 review card.

secure.text: You handled the talking patient correctly: patent airway for the moment, move to breathing, and reassess when things change.

shaky.text: You partly have the talking patient. A clear voice means a patent airway for now, so the next step is breathing, not intubation or skipping ahead, and ABCDE is repeated on any deterioration. GCS 8 or less triggers a definitive airway.

gap.text: The talking patient and the reassessment rule need rebuilding. Speech shows a patent airway only for the moment, so the next step is breathing, and you repeat ABCDE whenever the patient worsens. Revisit the O2 card and the GCS 8 trigger.

secure.text: You separated the adult and child surgical airway: surgical cricothyroidotomy in adults, needle in children under 12.

shaky.text: The adult and child airway rule is not steady yet. Surgical cricothyroidotomy suits adults; under about 12 years the cricoid is the only complete ring, so needle cricothyroidotomy is used. Check age before choosing.

gap.text: The emergency airway by age is a gap. Adults get surgical cricothyroidotomy; children under 12 get needle cricothyroidotomy because the cricoid ring is easily damaged. Read the O3 card and ask 'how old?' before any surgical airway.

secure.text: You treated tension pneumothorax clinically and at once: decompress first, no X-ray, no positive pressure, at the site the exam expects.

shaky.text: Tension pneumothorax is partly secure. It is a clinical diagnosis treated with immediate needle decompression then a chest tube, before X-ray or ventilation. Recheck the adult site (4th or 5th space, just in front of the mid-axillary line) against the older 2nd space key.

gap.text: Tension pneumothorax management is a gap. Diagnose it at the bedside, decompress immediately, then place a chest tube; do not wait for imaging and do not ventilate first. Learn both sites: PYQs expect the 2nd space mid-clavicular, ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th space. Review the O4 cards.

secure.text: You kept the chest look-alikes apart using percussion, neck veins, trachea and heart sounds.

shaky.text: Your chest contrasts are partly secure. Tension pneumothorax is hyper-resonant with distended neck veins; massive haemothorax is dull with flat veins; tamponade has muffled heart sounds with clear breath sounds. Redo the contrast table.

gap.text: The chest look-alikes are a gap. Absent breath sounds is shared, so it discriminates nothing. Use percussion and neck veins for air versus blood, heart sounds for tamponade, and remember hypoxia in flail chest comes from the contusion. Review the O5 cards.

secure.text: You read shock beyond blood pressure: tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure come first, hypotension is late, and age, drugs and neurogenic shock can mislead.

shaky.text: Shock recognition is partly secure. BP holds until Class III, and children, the elderly and beta-blocked patients can look normal while shocked. Slow pulse with warm skin points to neurogenic shock.

gap.text: Recognising shock is a gap. Hypotension first appears in Class III, 31 to 40 percent loss, so normal vitals do not clear children, the elderly, pregnancy or beta-blocked patients, and a slow pulse with warm skin is neurogenic shock. Review the O6 cards.

secure.text: You chose the current fluid plan: 1 L warmed crystalloid then early blood, and no permissive hypotension in brain injury.

shaky.text: Fluids are partly secure. ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in adults then early blood, while older keys said 2 L. Permissive hypotension does not apply with a brain injury.

gap.text: Initial fluids are a gap. Older keys expected 2 L; ATLS 10th edition says 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid then early blood. Permissive hypotension is not used in brain injury, which needs adequate perfusion. Review the O7 cards.

secure.text: You picked by stability and by sign: FAST for the unstable abdomen, and urethrogram before a catheter when urethral injury is possible.

shaky.text: This is partly secure. An unstable patient goes to FAST in the resuscitation room, not CT. With blood at the meatus or a high prostate, a urethrogram precedes the catheter.

gap.text: The investigation order is a gap. Unstable patients get FAST, not the CT scanner; suspected urethral injury needs a retrograde urethrogram before any catheter. Choose by stability and by the warning sign, not by test accuracy. Review the O8 cards.

secure.text: You placed the secondary survey correctly: only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way.

shaky.text: The secondary survey timing is a little uneven. It, with the AMPLE history, starts only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way.

gap.text: The secondary survey timing is a gap. Head-to-toe examination and AMPLE history start only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way. Read the O9 card.

secure.text: You gave tranexamic acid with the correct window, 3 hours from injury.

shaky.text: The tranexamic acid detail is shaky. The window is within 3 hours of injury; 8 hours is the length of the second infusion.

gap.text: Tranexamic acid is a gap. Give it within 3 hours of injury, 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours; the 8 is the infusion, not the window. Review the O10 card.

secure.text: You placed the trauma-death peaks correctly and matched ATLS to the second peak.

shaky.text: The peaks are shaky. First peak is seconds to minutes, second is minutes to hours (the one ATLS targets), third is days to weeks from sepsis.

gap.text: The peaks of trauma death are a gap. ATLS targets the second peak, minutes to several hours; sepsis belongs to the third. Pair each peak with an example and what can change it. Review the O11 card.

avoided.text: You ordered by speed of death, not by the loudest problem.

fell_recovered.text: You first put haemorrhage ahead of airway, then changed. Keep frequency (commonest preventable death) apart from priority (fastest killer). Military MARCH protocols do put bleeding first, but the ATLS exam order is ABCDE. This can return when blood is visible, so reread the order card.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but you have not yet shown it on a fresh question. Your model ranks by the most visible or common killer. Ask 'what kills in minutes' before 'what bleeds most': airway, then breathing, then circulation. Meet it again on the O1 review card.

avoided.text: You kept 'for the moment' attached to a talking patient.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated a talking patient as safe, then corrected. Speech shows a patent airway for now only; it can fail later, as with an expanding neck swelling. Repeat ABCDE with every change, especially under exam pressure.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not yet on a fresh question. Your model treats one good sign as a lasting all-clear. A talking patient has a patent airway only for the moment, so go to breathing and reassess on any change. See the O2 review card.

avoided.text: You treated tension pneumothorax at the bedside without waiting for imaging.

fell_recovered.text: You first asked for imaging before decompression, then changed. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; the patient cannot afford the delay. Shock plus the signs is enough, and the habit returns easily.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model applies 'image then treat' to a condition that kills before an image is taken. Bedside diagnosis is the top rung when shock is present. Meet it again on the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You chose by stability: FAST in the room for the unstable patient, CT for the stable one.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked CT for an unstable patient or treated FAST as organ-defining, then changed. Unstable goes to FAST or DPL; CT defines injury only in the stable patient. Recheck the ladder before the exam.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model equates the most accurate test with the first test. An unstable patient should not go to the scanner; FAST shows free fluid only. See the O8 review card.

avoided.text: You decompressed first rather than reaching for the tube.

fell_recovered.text: You first ventilated or intubated before decompressing, then changed. Positive pressure feeds a one-way valve and raises pressure. Decompress, then secure the airway; the letter order does not override the physiology.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model follows letters mechanically, so airway means a tube. Positive pressure pushes more air into a trapped space and impedes venous return. Trace the valve again on the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You read the pulse and skin, not only the pressure.

fell_recovered.text: You first called low pressure after trauma haemorrhagic, then changed. A slow pulse with warm dry skin points to neurogenic shock, while haemorrhage gives tachycardia. Hypovolaemia stays the default only until the pulse says otherwise.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stops at hypotension and calls it blood loss. Neurogenic shock gives hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin. Use the side-by-side contrast on the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You used percussion and neck veins to separate air from blood.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax as one picture, then changed. Both have absent breath sounds, so that finding separates nothing; hyper-resonance with full neck veins is air, dullness with flat veins is blood.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model treats any silent unilateral chest as one problem. Percuss and read the neck veins. Revisit the contrast on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You kept tamponade apart from tension pneumothorax using heart and breath sounds.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave Beck's triad to tension pneumothorax, then changed. Beck's triad is hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins; tamponade has clear breath sounds. Raised neck veins alone are shared.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stops at hypotension with raised neck veins. Check the heart sounds and the breath sounds. See the tamponade versus tension table on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You knew blood pressure is a late sign of haemorrhage.

fell_recovered.text: You first expected low BP early, then changed. Compensation holds systolic pressure until about a third of blood is lost, so hypotension first appears in Class III. Tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure come first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model assumes BP falls as soon as loss is moderate. Anchor to compensation: hypotension first appears in Class III, 31 to 40 percent. Revisit the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You gave the current fluid figure and knew why it changed.

fell_recovered.text: You first answered the older 2 L key, then changed. ATLS 10th edition says 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid, then early blood, because large volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient. Both keys exist, so read which edition the question follows.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model retrieves the number printed in older books. Old keys say 2 L; ATLS 10th edition says 1 L plus early blood. Note both on the O7 review card.

avoided.text: You gave the adult and child decompression sites correctly.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave the older 2nd space mid-clavicular site for an adult, then changed. ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th space just in front of the mid-axillary line in adults and keeps the 2nd space for children. Be ready for either key.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model holds the older memorised site without tying it to age or edition. PYQs expect the 2nd space; ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th for adults. Write both on the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You linked flail chest hypoxia to the contusion, not the moving segment.

fell_recovered.text: You first blamed the paradoxical movement for the hypoxia, then changed. The visible sign defines the injury, but the underlying pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment is oxygen, analgesia and cautious fluids.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model takes the sign for the cause, so you would treat the movement, not the lung. The contusion drives the hypoxia. See the flail chest part of the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You pictured pressure pushing the mediastinum away from the tension side.

fell_recovered.text: You first reversed the shift, then changed. Trapped air under pressure pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side and kinks the great veins; a collapsed lung does not pull them over.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model pictures the collapse pulling the trachea toward the injured side. Trace the valve, rising pressure, push to the opposite side. Redo the mechanism on the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You doubted normal vitals in the groups that blunt them.

fell_recovered.text: You first trusted normal vital signs in a qualifier patient, then changed. Beta-blockers and age blunt the pulse, children hold pressure until late, and pregnancy hides up to about a third of blood volume. Check the qualifier first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model uses normal vitals as default reassurance. Check age, pregnancy and drugs every time before accepting them. Compare the two patients on the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You checked age before choosing a surgical airway.

fell_recovered.text: You first used the adult surgical airway in a child, then changed. Under about 12 years use needle cricothyroidotomy, because the cricoid is the only complete ring and is easily damaged. Check age whenever a surgical airway is on the table.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model applies the adult rule to a child. Ask the age: adult surgical, child under 12 needle cricothyroidotomy. See the O3 review card.

avoided.text: You looked for urethral injury signs before catheterising.

fell_recovered.text: You first catheterised in a patient with possible urethral injury, then changed. Blood at the meatus or a high-riding prostate means a retrograde urethrogram first. The routine catheter is the habit to watch.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model treats the catheter as automatic. Scan for meatal blood, perineal bruising and a high prostate, then urethrogram, then catheter. See the O8 review card.

avoided.text: You matched ATLS to the second peak of trauma deaths.

fell_recovered.text: You first linked ATLS to the third peak, then changed. ATLS targets the second peak, minutes to hours after injury, where resuscitation can change the outcome; sepsis and organ failure are the third.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model links the most familiar late cause of death to ATLS. Pair each peak with what can change it. See the O11 review card.

avoided.text: You held the five life-threatening chest injuries, tamponade included.

fell_recovered.text: You first built the chest list loosely, then changed. The five are tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with contusion, and tamponade assessed under circulation. Simple pneumothorax is not one of them.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model stores chest injuries as a vague pile and drops tamponade. Rebuild the five from oxygenation, ventilation and filling. See the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You checked for a head injury before accepting low pressure.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied permissive hypotension in a head-injured patient, then changed. It is not used in traumatic brain injury, where the brain needs adequate perfusion. Check for a head injury first.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model applies the haemorrhage rule to everyone. Ask whether the brain needs a higher perfusion pressure. See the O7 review card.

avoided.text: You separated the 3-hour window from the 8-hour infusion.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave tranexamic acid on the 8-hour figure, then changed. Start within 3 hours of injury; 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours is the regimen, and 8 is its duration, not its window.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected on the spot, but not on a fresh question. Your model files the memorable number under the wrong label. The window is 3 hours; the infusion is 8. See the O10 review card.

E1.text: You tend to merge look-alikes: shared findings such as absent breath sounds or low pressure feel like one picture. Before naming a diagnosis, find the one sign that only one condition has (percussion, neck veins, pulse, heart sounds).

E2.text: You tend to build lists loosely, adding familiar items or dropping the odd one out. Rebuild a set from its logic, then test it with 'which is NOT'.

E3.text: You tend to reverse direction or cause: sign for cause, collapse for pressure. Predict what happens step by step from the mechanism before choosing.

E4.text: You tend to stretch a reassuring sign beyond its qualifier. Reread the exact words, such as 'for the moment', and ask when the sign could fail.

E5.text: You tend to answer with the older exam key. Learn both: what PYQs expected and what ATLS 10th edition says, with the reason for the change.

E6.text: You tend to swap numbers, attaching a figure to the wrong label such as window versus infusion or class versus percentage. Anchor each number to what it means, then retest it in a case.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier: age, drug, pregnancy or brain injury. Before using a rule, ask who this patient is and whether the rule has an exception.

E8.text: You tend to pick the test or step by accuracy or routine, not by stability and warning signs. Ask first whether this patient can afford the delay and whether a sign forbids the routine.

E9.text: You tend to get priorities wrong, choosing by what is visible, common or the first letter. Order by time to death and by physiology, then decide.

E10.text: You tend to attach a fact to the nearest familiar item, such as sepsis to ATLS. Pair each item with its own example and what can change it.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on two or more answers that were wrong. Those are the most useful errors, since a confident error corrected is remembered well. Do their review cards first, and before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or discriminating sign that makes you certain.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on several answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, say the reason before you tap, and if it holds, tap Sure.

calibrated.text: Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure answers were mostly right and doubt appeared where you missed. That is a useful exam skill, so keep tagging answers honestly.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. That is fine while learning, but unaided recall is what the exam tests. Revisit the cards for the objectives where you asked, and answer first before opening help.

hints_none.text: You asked for no hints, so your misses were real recall gaps rather than missing information. Use the review cards to refill those, then retest without help.

hinted_only.text: On some objectives you were right only after a hint. Treat those as not yet secure: redo their review cards and answer cold before opening any help.

fast_lane.text: You skipped at least one lesson, such as the ABCDE order, the peaks recap, the worked shock cases or the management plan, and went straight to the questions. Skipping is a fair call, but it does not show mastery. Review the cards for those skipped lessons.

gap.text: Start with the review cards for objectives marked gap, and confident errors first. Do one card per sitting, say the discriminating feature or qualifier aloud, then retest on a fresh question. Revisit the fell-open items after a day.

clear.text: No objective is a gap. Space the review cards over the next days and weeks, and rehearse both keys for the old-versus-ATLS 10th edition items so they hold under exam pressure.
